While the Trump administration has advanced key priorities such as tax cuts, deregulation, and the use of tariffs as leverage over trading partners, comprehensive reform of the immigration system has proved more difficult, even if it has increased enforcement.

“What I hear from our clients and customers is that they want to be able to figure their way through on immigration. They want to know what the rules are going to be so that they can adjust their business models,” Moynihan said.

“Construction companies all over the country, farmers and hospitals are saying, ‘I need workers. I used to get them this way, but I’m not getting them through this way. So, how are we going to figure this out’?”

While some argue that natural population growth in the US is the answer, Moynihan said: “It takes 18 years to make an 18-year-old. So, you’re not going to have a change in population in the United States of any consequence. It’s going to be an interesting debate.”

He said there was still “a lot of work to be done” on reaching new trade deals with Canada and Mexico. Relations with both neighbours have become more volatile and strained, with Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, in particular, turning more confrontational over the summer.

Major news outlets from Bloomberg to the Washington Post have reported that US business leaders have, by contrast, been reluctant to criticise Trump publicly during his second presidency, fearing retaliation or risking access to the White House.

The CEO of America’s second-largest bank, with $3.5 trillion of assets, has likewise avoided directly challenging the president. Perhaps his most pointed intervention came in a CBS interview last December, when asked about political interference with the Fed as Trump was openly attacking its rates policy. “The market will punish people if we don’t have an independent Fed,” he warned.” And everybody knows that.”

The cautious approach hasn’t spared Moynihan Trump’s ire – or the occasional cold shoulder.

Three days after his second inauguration in January 2025, Trump used a video address to the World Economic Forum in Davos to scold the Bank of America boss and JP Morgan chief Jamie Dimon over allegations that their banks were denying services to – or “debanking” – conservative customers.

“He was saying that people weren’t banking people because they believe X, Y, or Z. We honestly don’t believe that’s correct,” said Moynihan.

Moynihan was the only CEO of a major Wall Street bank not to be invited to a reception honouring Trump when he attended Davos earlier this year, according to a Financial Times report at the time, months after he was left off the list for a dinner of banking executives at a White House event last November.

Asked how history will judge Trump’s economic legacy, Moynihan was circumspect.

“I think it will take time,” he said, noting that tax cuts for workers and new provisions allowing companies to deduct certain investment costs more quickly have boosted economic activity. But it will take years to determine whether the gains are sustainable, Moynihan added.

Bank of America’s Dublin EU hub sees profits dip to $1.76bn in 2024

He was keen to emphasise how his group, whose roots date back to the founding in 1784 of The Massachusetts Bank, has helped administrations through the centuries. “We’re here to serve every administration,” he said.

Yet the new $1.2 billion fine marks a low point in the bank’s relationship with the current one. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said as he announced the penalty.

It has left Moynihan, CEO since 2010, facing fresh scrutiny of the bank’s processes and controls, having spent the early years of his time at the helm resolving legal and regulatory claims stemming from the US housing and mortgages bubble that collapsed in 2007–2008.

Asked by analysts during a conference call on Wednesday about “how it gets to this point” and whether there was a misunderstanding of the rules, he said: “I think at the end of the day, we understand what they need us to do. We’re deep in the process of remediating.”

Irish-American background

Moynihan, whose ancestors emigrated from Ireland in the 1850s, was born in Marietta, Ohio, where his father worked as a research chemist with DuPont. The second-youngest of eight siblings, he earned a Bachelor of Arts in 1981 from Brown, where he co-captained the rugby team and met his future wife, classmate Susan Berry.

After securing a law degree from the University of Notre Dame in 1984, he took a position at Rhode Island-based law firm Edwards and Angell. One of his clients was Fleet Financial in Boston, which lured him nine years later to become its deputy general counsel.

Moynihan would wear many hats at the company before and after its 1999 merger with local rival BankBoston. He was managing FleetBoston’s wealth and investment management division when it was taken over in 2004 by Charlotte, North Carolina-based Bank of America.

The global economy and the art of living dangerously

Bank of America’s then-CEO, Ken Lewis, tapped him to become president of the enlarged group’s wealth management business. He appointed him as the group’s general counsel in December 2008, just before Bank of America completed its rescue takeover – albeit for a price of $50 billion – of Merrill Lynch, one of Wall Street’s most storied names. Less than a month after the deal was sealed, Merrill Lynch’s former CEO John Thain resigned and was replaced by Moynihan as president of global banking, wealth and investment management.

Moynihan – who speaks quietly and sometimes mumbles – was a surprise choice to lead the group in late 2009. The board was known to have been searching for an outside star after Lewis resigned amid a shareholder backlash following the disastrous Merrill deal.

EU hub post Brexit

Bank of America chose Dublin as its EU headquarters in 2017 in the wake of the Brexit referendum. The unit has two main divisions: global banking and markets, and support services, which includes a global technology and operations centre.

The US banking giant has had a presence in the Republic since 1968. It has more than 1,000 employees in Dublin and about 400 contractors.

The group opened a new office in Belfast late last year and announced last week that it had hired more than 300 staff there, initially focused on anti-money laundering and financial crime compliance. It has a goal of creating up to 1,000 roles in the North.

“We knew the talent was there. We knew that there was capacity, with office space and other things we could get. And it’s a city that’s continuing to grow,” Moynihan said. “We knew we were going to have to expand this business, because it always grows when the business grows.”

All told, Bank of America has about 210,000 employees across 35 countries – broadly the same headcount as in 2007, even though it took on about 76,000 staff through its 2008 acquisitions of Merrill Lynch and mortgage lender Countrywide Financial.

Moynihan has said that Bank of America’s ongoing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is focused on getting more out of its workforce rather than cutting jobs. The bank has rolled out around 150 AI use cases across the group so far, with “hundreds” more in the pipeline, he said.

He said there is little room for error when rolling out AI to customers, because trust, security and reliability are fundamental to a banking relationship.

“If we used it to make loans, and it turned somebody down, and they alleged we turned them down because of whatever non-valid credit-based decision ... and the [AI agent] couldn’t explain its work, that’s where the agents are going to be tricky to implement.”

Moynihan declined to be dragged into the AI bubble debate, deferring to research last week from the bank’s market strategists, who noted that a narrow group of AI companies has been driving the Nasdaq 100 Index to all-time highs recently. “Low breadth is a classic feature of bubbles building and typically doesn’t stop until they pop,” they said.

Profit surge

Bank of America’s shares surged more than fourfold between Moynihan taking charge in 2010 and mid-August. Its annual profits grew at a similar pace even as total assets rose by only 60 per cent. The $1.2 billion fine – while embarrassing – equates to about 3.6 per cent of the group’s net income for the 12 months to the end of September, and has only brought the stock back to where it was in late May.

The CEO lives in Wellesley, Massachusetts, an affluent suburb west of Boston, and divides his working time between Boston and the group’s headquarters in Charlotte.

Succession planning moved up a notch 13 months ago when the bank promoted two executives – Dean Athanasia and Jim DeMare – to co-presidents of the entire business, and chief financial officer Alastair Borthwick was given the title of executive vice-president.

But Moynihan was coy when asked how long he planned to stick around.

“I don’t talk about it,” he said. “But I expect to serve as long as the board will have me and I’m having fun.”

CV

Name: Brian Moynihan.

Job: CEO of Bank of America.

Age: 67.

Family: Married to Susan Berry, whom he met at college, with three adult children.

Lives: Wellesley, near Boston in Massachusetts.

Something you might expect: He is chancellor of Brown University, where he previously studied.

Something that might surprise: He reportedly likes to amuse himself by slipping obscure, archaic words such as “fantods”, “fructify”, “gainsay”, and “concomitant” into calls with analysts.

]]>Clodagh Kilcoyne<![CDATA[Fiscal advisers point out the flaws but Government ignores them. What’s the point of Ifac?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/what-is-the-point-of-ifac-if-the-coalition-just-ignores-its-warnings/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/what-is-the-point-of-ifac-if-the-coalition-just-ignores-its-warnings/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 04:15:00 +0000All bark and no bite. If you wanted to be cruel about Ireland’s so-called fiscal watchdog – that would be the obvious cliche to throw its way.

For years, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) has advised successive ministers for finance to go easy on the spending increases and tax cuts, put away more money and account properly for the possibility of overruns.

Yet, time and again on budget day, much of the advice appears to be quietly ignored.

Take Budget 2027, for example.

The budgetary process now begins several months before the big day itself – with the Stability Programme Update in April, followed by the Summer Economic Statement (SES) in July. Between them, the two documents provide a good sense of what will be at the Government’s disposal later in the year.

In August, after having a good look at the SES, which outlined the broad parameters for the budget, Ifac said the economy did not need any budgetary support.

It said the economy continued to grow at a “remarkable pace” even when the distorting impact of the multinationals was stripped out of the official figures.

Casting his eye across the SES’s implied net spending growth, its chairman Seamus Coffey said the plans were “not appropriate” for an economy in such a strong position.

Ifac’s position was that if the Government continued down this road, then its policies would only add to an already worrying inflation outlook.

And what did the Government do?

Within hours of the budget’s publication, Ifac said it had put “the public finances on a worse trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.

Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns

Coffey noted that, rather than heed the warnings, the Government was planning on spending €6 out of every €7 in corporation tax it collected.

The Government, as would be expected, defended the €8.7 billion in new measures. Minister for Finance Simon Harris had already defined the respective roles as he saw it.

“We don’t ignore their advice, but they’re not the Government,” he said.

So what is the continued point of having an institution set up in the wake of the 2008 crash to prevent a re-run of that calamity if modern-day governments choose not to take its advice?

Michael McMahon, a professor of macroeconomics, sat on the council for nearly seven years before serving as interim chairman between 2023 and 2024.

“When I joined, I thought we’d actually be advising the Government,” he says.

“That we’d go and meet the ministers involved and say, ‘This is a nonsensical policy; we think this would be better’. I thought it would be technocratic, geeky advice on the highest levels.”

Instead, McMahon quickly realised it was Ifac’s role to assess what was being proposed. “You could replace the word ‘advisory’ in Ifac’s name with ‘assessment’,” he says.

While chairman in 2023, McMahon added his voice to those of his predecessors, warning that the government risked “repeating Ireland’s past mistakes” with its upcoming budget. In particular, the tendency to breach its own spending rule had bothered the council members.

At the time, he said the State was over-reliant on windfall corporation tax revenues in the same way pre-crash governments had relied on property-related taxes.

How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents

McMahon also entertained the idea that, at some point in the future, Ifac could hit the “big red button” available to it and refuse to endorse budgetary forecasts. He said the council would be more likely to “wield big sticks” if the spending breaches were going to be repeated year after year.

Looking back, did his words and those of the other Ifac members have any impact?

“The question is not whether the government has always exactly complied with the letter of the recommendations,” he says.

“But rather, what would have happened with spending and tax decisions if an institution like the fiscal council was not endorsing the macro forecasts and criticising the decisions being made?”

McMahon says it is likely, in his view, that government spending would have been higher- and potentially riskier – had it not been for the role played by Ifac over a number of years.

During his time on the council, the government consistently ignored its own spending growth cap of 5 per cent annually, exceeding it each time.

However, the economist claims the cap may not have been introduced at all or, if it had, it would have been exceeded by an even greater margin had there been no independent oversight.

“It’s a very difficult thing to assess,” he says.

“I personally felt over the time I was there, it was a kind of slow beating of a drum of messages that were getting through. Questions were being asked in the media about growing spending at 6 and 7 per cent when their target was 5 per cent.”

McMahon also says it is his belief that the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) – the sovereign wealth fund into which the Government is investing 0.8 per cent of GDP annually – may not have come about had it not been for persistent calls for such a plan from Ifac.

“I think Ifac is useful; it has shifted the debate in Ireland. I don’t think we would have the FIF without it,” he says.

Ifac was established during the bailout years, when the country was picking up the pieces from an economic crash that pushed us into a three-year IMF-EU bailout.

Cut costs and abolish Ifac

Ireland had narrowed its tax base during the Celtic Tiger era and was badly caught out when the international banking crisis coincided with a collapse in house prices. An over-dependence on elements like stamp duty left public finances cruelly exposed.

Ifac, it appeared, was designed to remind policymakers that the same mistakes could not be repeated. Promoting fiscal responsibility seemed to be its overarching mission.

John Moran was secretary general at the Department of Finance between 2012 and 2014 when Ifac first got up and running. The terms of the bailout hung over the government, and the council was, at times, insistent on difficult medicine.

“We were in a tough position of trying to bring the budget back into order,” he says.

“There would have been moments of disagreement [with Ifac], where perhaps the political judgment of the government at the time was that they needed to do things that were seen as more politically palatable to keep the coalition together and keep the public onside.”

Moran says the economic landscape nowadays, in some ways, is comparable to the pre-crisis years.

“Today’s world is in a different position,” he says. “There are questions about how much extra spending you can do; that’s where the contrast lies [with the bailout years].

“We have some parallels between now and the situation before when we got into financial difficulties, with very concentrated tax sources.”

Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice

The first chairman of Ifac was Prof John McHale.

He believes its importance lies in being able to publicise a counterpoint to government policy. Much of the time, he says, what Ifac is stating is not entirely different from what senior civil servants are telling ministers behind the scenes.

“It is different from [saying] it in public. In a way it helps the government – it helps balance the debate,” McHale says.

“You would never expect the government would take on what we would advise wholesale – it’s under huge political pressure. The council’s role was to take on a longer-term view. We were pulling in very different directions.”

So what was the relationship like between the government and Ifac?

“On the whole, it was good. Sometimes they were a little less forthcoming with information than the council would have liked, and it made our job harder,” he says.

That inability to always get the information it wants from civil servants could be solved, says McHale, by granting Ifac a statutory right. He points out that the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has again recently called for this.

That report also highlighted the relative lack of resources available to the council.

Applauding its ability to shape the media narrative here, the OECD said the body “punches above its weight”. It said Ifac ranked highly among similar bodies in other countries and had an ability to “generate influence despite limited resources”.

While winning plaudits from external reviewers, some politicians have eyed Ifac with a little suspicion over the years.

At a time when Ireland was crying out for public investment, particularly in housing, it has been accused of sometimes offering a narrow and needlessly cautious prescription. Yes, the argument went, the economy is doing well, but there are huge gaps where more money should also be spent.

How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in?

Sinn Féin’s spokesman on finance, Pearse Doherty, says there could be “question marks” over some of Ifac’s warnings down through the years, which were perhaps “too conservative”.

“If we look back at Ifac’s recommendations – and they have gone unheeded by the government in the past – the economy has still continued to grow and continued to have surpluses,” he says.

However, he says the council has played an important role over recent budgets in highlighting consistent spending overruns.

“Ifac have focused – and I think they have been misrepresented in my own view – on the government’s unplanned spending,” he says.

“It undermines the budget day process. You have a situation where the government announces X amount of spending on budget day, but by the end of the year, that has gone up due to unplanned measures.”

Doherty says he doesn’t know what Ifac would have to say about his party’s budget plans. But he believes it would be in line with Ifac’s current thinking on how the funding of extra spending should be done through the raising of additional tax revenues.

“The big difference between us and the Government is that we would increase capital expenditure,” he says. “I’m not sure what view they (Ifac) would take in relation to that.”

The other question that gets thrown at the “watchdog” is whether it is still needed, given that bodies such as the Central Bank of Ireland and the ESRI frequently offer similar criticisms of budgetary policy. The groupthink that prevailed in the pre-crisis period, so the argument goes, is no longer a problem.

With so much cash sloshing around, why is there a housing crisis?

“It is certainly true that there is a lot of common ground between the ESRI, the council and the Central Bank,” says McHale.

“It makes a difference when you have a body that has a statutory role in assessing these things. The Government has to respond to the council’s report; that is what really makes it stand out.”

McHale, though no longer part of Ifac, believes that budgetary policy is in a “reasonable place”. Despite criticisms around the nature of windfall taxes, he says it remains important that the Government is still running surpluses, though he’d like these to be higher.

This would be wise, he says, “given the underlying risks we face”.

McMahon says Ifac is more about “shaping thinking than shaping policies” and it fits the role of a “town crier”.

“We would all love 10 per cent growth a year, and everyone get free cookies,” he says.

“But we all know the pain that comes from reckless fiscal policy, and there is generally more pain than there is fun on the upside.”

]]><![CDATA[Third word error in Aer Lingus disciplinary papers, WRC is told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/third-word-error-in-aer-lingus-disciplinary-papers-wrc-is-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/third-word-error-in-aer-lingus-disciplinary-papers-wrc-is-told/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 09:48:03 +0000The case of an Aer Lingus pilot who says he should not have been stripped of command responsibility for failing to immediately file an air safety report over what he considered a “non-event” has heard of a third word error in internal company documents on the case.

Hearings on complaints by Declan McCabe under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 are continuing this week at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

The WRC has heard for the third time of what is said to be an error in wording in internal company documents concerning a disciplinary process brought against McCabe.

The tribunal was told on Thursday that when the airline’s chief pilot wrote that McCabe had been “indicted” by a safety investigation, he meant to write “indicated”.

McCabe was disciplined for what the airline deemed breaches of his air safety reporting obligations while flying in command of an Airbus A321xlr, which failed to link up with a radio navigation beacon coming into Dublin Airport before making a turn to re-establish contact.

Aer Lingus pilot ‘uncomfortable’ at crossing picket line to attend WRC hearing

The conclusion in a disciplinary investigation was that McCabe’s aircraft, with 156 passengers and crew aboard, was “flying in the wrong direction ... until air traffic control intervened” on the day, according to Captain Eamon Kierans, the manager who conducted the process.

McCabe said what happened was “a non-event from a flying point of view” and that the relevant Aer Lingus manual left it up to his judgment to decide whether to report it. The company disagreed, and while his actions as a pilot were not impugned, the airline concluded he had failed in his safety reporting duties by not filing a report until he was directed to do so by the airline’s director of safety and security Conor Nolan.

The tribunal heard that Capt Nolan decided in a safety review that the flight crew’s actions prior to the air safety report being submitted amounted to a “reckless violation” – leading ultimately to disciplinary action.

McCabe’s case is that the airline had no right to pursue a disciplinary process against him and that it was penalisation for complaining about another senior managing pilot, Capt Colm Wynne, having a safety management role in the airline, on foot of a previous dispute dating back to 2011.

Yvonne De Silva, who was director of in-flight services at Aer Lingus in 2024, upheld the disciplinary sanction against McCabe when she gave her decision on his internal appeal in March 2024.

David Byrnes BL, for the complainant, said that during the appeal stage his client argued that the entire disciplinary process was prejudged. McCabe cited a letter from the airline’s then-chief pilot, Capt John Kelly, stating before the disciplinary process began that McCabe was “already indicted” by Capt Nolan’s safety probe.

Giving evidence, De Silva said the only role Capt Kelly had in relation to her appeal process had been to ask about her availability, and that she had been assigned to the process by Aer Lingus HR.

“You know what indictment means – charges brought before even a disciplinary investigation to say that a disciplinary hearing is warranted,” Byrnes asked the witness.

“Yes,” De Silva replied. She said she had agreed with McCabe that the word “indictment” was “not appropriate” when he brought it up at appeal stage.

“I read the email myself. My interpretation was that it was a typo,” De Silva said.

McCabe told her at the appeal that Capt Kelly “hadn’t mentioned it”, she said.

“I spoke to captain Kelly and mentioned what was his thinking. He said: ‘Oh, that was a typo; when I wrote back to him I didn’t notice the typo myself,’” De Silva said.

“I wrote in my outcome letter that it was a typo, it was my view that it was a typo,” she said. “The use of the word ‘indicted’ was a typo on the part of captain Kelly – it should have said ‘indicated’” .

Her finding was that “having read the full email, there was no other logical conclusion”.

Earlier this year, Capt Conor Barrett, the disciplinary investigator in McCabe’s case, said he used the word “believe” when he meant to write “belie” in relation to McCabe’s interpretation of the manual’s safety reporting section.

Capt Barrett told the WRC the next day that when he used the word “belies” elsewhere in the report, he meant something different. De Silva said she mentioned the typo in the course of a broader discussion with Capt Kelly – one of a number of conversations she had with senior pilots at the airline during the appeal process, she said.

She told the WRC she wanted “to get a little bit more information” from them.

Byrnes asked De Silva: “Did you document these conversations?”

“No,” she said.

“I believed it was the right thing to do,” De Silva said.

Byrnes said his client was entitled to “know the evidence and test the evidence from the start to the bitter end” but had only found out about these conversations for the first time at the WRC on Thursday.

Counsel said the information gleaned from such conversations “clearly materially influenced” the appeal process and asked De Silva to show him where the Aer Lingus policy provided for her to have such discussions without notice to the appellant.

“You’re probably going to tell me it’s not there,” De Silva said.

Counsel said De Silva “showed bias toward what people outside the process were telling you”, which she denied.

Byrnes asked her whether she told his client that one of the people she spoke with in this context was Capt Kierans, the disciplinary officer, and “the person you were reviewing in this appeal”.

“No,” De Silva said.

Byrnes asked whether the HR officer assisting De Silva with the appeal process had warned her that she “ought to be careful” about contacting Kierans during the appeal.

“I can’t remember,” De Silva said. She accepted she did not give McCabe and his representative during the internal process, Capt Padraig Higgins, “a chance to respond to those conversations I had”.

The case continues.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445039/">
   <title>Huthis bauen Rakete unabhängig von Iran</title>
   <description>Im Zuge des Iran-Krieges, den die USA und Israel Ende Februar begonnen haben, ist auch der Konflikt im Jemen wieder eskaliert. Dabei konnte die proiranische Huthi-Miliz weitere Gebiete einnehmen. Die von Saudi-Arabien angeführte Militärkoalition bekämpft die Huthis, die Miliz greift im Gegenzug täglich strategisch wichtige Ziele in Saudi-Arabien an, erst am Sonntag wieder. Zugleich wird laut einem aktuellen Bericht der Bau einer eigenen Version der iranischen Mittelstreckenrakete Cheibar Schekan vorangetrieben.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444830/">
   <title>Neuer Balkan-Pop inmitten alter Konflikte</title>
   <description>Der Westbalkan hat einen neuen Popstar: Der 21-jährige Kroate Jakov Jozinovic füllt Hallen in der Region und trat am Samstag erstmals nahe Wien auf. Bekannt wurde er mit Neuinterpretationen beliebter Balkan-Klassiker. Doch ein Video, das ihn beim Singen eines Liedes des rechtsextremen kroatischen Musikers Thompson zeigt, löste Mitte Oktober heftige Proteste aus. Jozinovic erklärte, er habe „niemanden verletzen wollen“, der Vorfall entfacht erneut Debatten über nationale Identität und die Aufarbeitung der Vergangenheit auf dem Balkan.</description>

Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.

Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.

#Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨

📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC.

🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej.

🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol

— Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026

Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.

 

From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.

Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.

In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.

Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026

In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.

With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.

While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.

The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.

“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”

Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

]]> Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/16/poland-drops-proposal-to-criminalise-providing-help-to-illegal-migrants-following-outcry/ Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:38:51 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105617

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.

The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026

Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.

However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.

“Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily.

 

That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus.

Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers.

Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross.

However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support.

Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025

In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”.

The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability.

“This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily.

Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022.

A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025

They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted.

On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”.

Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition.

‼️ Ciepły posiłek, nocleg, potrzebne leki – za to wolontariusz ma trafić do więzienia nawet na 3 lata? 😡 Nie ma zgody Lewicy na kryminalizowanie pomocy humanitarnej!

Ministra Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk zwróciła się do ministra Waldemara Żurka ze stanowczym sprzeciwem wobec… pic.twitter.com/QskUfJmgsu

— Lewica (@__Lewica) October 14, 2026

In response to the growing criticism, the interior ministry announced on Friday that it was withdrawing the proposal, saying it decided to do so “to eliminate any doubts and prevent the misinterpretation of regulations”.

“From the beginning, the ministry’s sole objective has been to tighten the system and target the organisers of this practice [of migrant smuggling],” said the ministry, quoted by Rzeczpospolita.

“Legal provisions must effectively protect the state’s borders against organised crime, while simultaneously fully safeguarding humanitarian values ​and life-saving activities.”

The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%

Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026

Both the former Polish government and the current one, which took power in December 2023, have regularly faced criticism from human rights groups over their response to the migration crisis on the Belarus border.

Earlier this year, the previous human rights commissioner, Marcin Wiącek, expressed concern over a ban on asylum claims introduced by the government in March 2025. He noted that the measures had been described as a temporary solution, but have remained in place ever since.

The government, however, argues that its measures have been effective in preventing the illegal trafficking of migrants. Its data show that attempted border crossings from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%.

It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally.

]]> Heads of Polish and Ukrainian national remembrance institutes hold first meeting since 2018 https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/16/heads-of-polish-and-ukrainian-national-remembrance-institutes-hold-first-meeting-since-2018/ Fri, 16 Oct 2026 09:30:54 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105570

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years.

The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies.

📢 14 października 2026 r. we Lwowie delegacja Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej spotkała się z przedstawicielami ukraińskiego Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r.

➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa

— Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026

News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”.

The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov.

“The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions.

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026

Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian).

At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people.

The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2

It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians.

There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set.

 

This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes.

In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”.

By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide.

In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres.

The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups.

Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism

It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025

In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry.

However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle.

Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”.

]]> Ukraine finds remains of 30 people in search for victims of massacre by Polish WWII partisans https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/15/ukraine-finds-remains-of-30-people-in-search-for-victims-of-massacre-by-polish-wwii-partisans/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 13:43:10 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105569

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two.

The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history.

Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war.

At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine.

On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population.

Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk.

On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there.

Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026

Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″.

Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”.

“Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.”

“True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery.

 

At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers.

Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”.

“This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.”

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026

The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children.

Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war.

In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations.

The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”.

He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026

Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims.

Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024.

The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues.

As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy.

The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

1294/2026

Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo

— Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026

Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him.

However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government).

Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS.

In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions.

Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026

Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal.

Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog.

So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK.

Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026

Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry.

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”.

However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”.

This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force.

Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine.

“In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre.

The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries.

Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries.

Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.

“The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.”

 

The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”.

Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors.

Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe.

“Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine.
